newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian army battles rebels, West in peace drive.
newsitem.headline: Albanian army battles rebels, West in peace drive.

text.p: Albania's army has clashed with rebels in volatile southern regions in its drive to extinguish resistance to President Sali Berisha.
Western countries mounted a campaign on Wednesday to end the violence which has killed at least 20 people in the past week.

A delegation from the Council of Europe, a pan-European organisation which promotes democracy and human rights, arrived for talks and a European Union mission headed by the Dutch foreign minister was due on Friday.
Albanian opposition groups, generally demoralised by the imposition of emergency rule last weekend, issued an appeal to the West to persuade Berisha to accept a political settlement.
Tirana authorities portrayed life as normal throughout the impoverished Balkan country.
Witnesses saw the army withdraw in trucks after 40 minutes of fighting with armed groups east of the port of Sarande, near the Greek border.
They saw at least four fighters and two soldiers hurt and hospital officials said one man was in a serious condition.
"The people won. The army, about 60 soldiers, got in their trucks and drove away," Sarande's former prefect Dimitris Stefos told Reuters in Athens by telephone.

One wounded insurgent told reporters the army had operated under the shoot-on-sight order which went into effect on Monday, the same day parliament re-elected Berisha to a second term. The assembly, where Berisha's Democratic Party holds nearly all the seats, had introduced the state of emergency the previous day.
Sarande residents, contacted from Athens, said rebels staged an evening rally in a main square, defying a curfew, and held guns and babies aloft while chanting anti-government slogans.
Army tanks and armoured personnel carriers roamed roads near the main regional town of Gjirokaster, 30 km (18 miles) north of the border, a Reuters correspondent in the area reported.

The Health Ministry in Tirana said two people had died from gunfire in the port of Vlore further north -- site of some of the fiercest clashes sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment funds with the life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians.
Anger over the failed pyramid schemes has spread across the country and at the weekend rioters burned and looted in the border region. They stole thousands of arms from state arsenals.
The capital remained quiet, though armed police patrolled squares and intersections. Berisha suggested cutting the overnight curfew by three hours in Tirana and other unaffected towns.
State television showed shops and services operating normally throughout the country of 3.2 million.
"It was hard to distinguish today from any normal day," a reporter said of the town of Kavaje, west of Tirana. "Food and water supplies are normal, but prices rose two to five percent."
Television also showed what it said was an arsenal of 4,500 weapons handed in by residents of Fier, another southern flashpoint of recent disturbances.

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said his Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo had spoken to Berisha earlier on Wednesday and would fly to Tirana on Friday to convey a firm message on behalf of the European Union.

"We are naturally strongly in favour of a political solution. We are in continuous contact with several capitals, notably Athens, because the Greek government is very much concerned by developments," Kok said after talks in Paris with French President Jacques Chirac.
The Netherlands is the current holder of the EU's six-month rotating presidency.
"I can only hope that the Albanian president will find the possibility of a political solution to this problem because what is going on and what could happen there is really tragic," Kok said.

The leader of the Council of Europe delegation to Albania, Dutch Christian Democrat Rene van der Linden, said he planned to put pressure on the government and the opposition to open a dialogue to end the crisis.

"Albania is a member of the Council of Europe since 1995 and it assumed a number of obligations -- ensuring the rule of law, human rights, freedom of the media and so on," he told British Broadcasting Corporation radio.
"The government is entitled to restore law and order but its forces, including the secret police, must do so in accordance with the law and international standards."
Van der Linden said Albania's membership of the Council of Europe would be at risk if Berisha did not implement the group's rules.
